title: Swinton v. Whitinsville Savings Bank
summary: The Massachusetts court rejected a damages claim based only on a seller’s silence about a concealed termite infestation, while distinguishing affirmative deception and duties to disclose.
notes: The sale took place on September 12, 1938 and the infestation was discovered on August 30, 1940; the decision (311 Mass. 677, 42 N.E.2d 808) is the standard statement of caveat emptor: absent a false statement, a fiduciary relationship or a special duty to speak, a seller's silence about a known, non-obvious defect in an arm's-length sale is not actionable.

sections.Parties: Swinton bought a house from Whitinsville Savings Bank. He sued the bank for the costs associated with its termite infestation.
sections.Material Facts:
The complaint alleged that the bank knew the house was infested when it sold the property for use as a family home in 1938. The infestation could not readily be observed on inspection. Swinton alleged that he learned of it in 1940 and incurred substantial repair and termite-control expenses.

The complaint did not allege a false affirmative statement, a misleading half-truth, interference with investigation, a fiduciary relationship, or a relationship of special confidence or dependence. Its allegation of fraudulent concealment consisted of the failure to reveal the condition during an arm’s-length sale.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court sustained the bank’s demurrer, which challenged the legal sufficiency of the complaint. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court affirmed and directed judgment for the bank. The facts were alleged rather than established after a trial.
sections.Issue: Did knowledge of a latent defect, without an additional duty or act of deception, make the seller liable for failing to disclose it?
sections.Holding: No, under the Massachusetts rule applied in this 1942 decision. Bare nondisclosure did not state the asserted cause of action.
sections.Reasoning:
The court defined the issue narrowly by identifying what the complaint did not allege. A general characterization of silence as fraudulent could not replace facts establishing a duty to speak. The parties were ordinary buyer and seller, and the seller had neither made a misleading statement nor prevented the buyer from obtaining information.

The court feared that liability on these allegations would require every seller to reveal all known hidden defects and, by parallel reasoning, every buyer to reveal hidden value known only to the buyer. It declined to impose that general disclosure regime. It acknowledged the hardship of an unfamiliar concealed hazard but did not create a termite-specific exception.

The following notes describe statutes and decisions in other jurisdictions that impose broader disclosure or warranty obligations. This case must therefore be read with its historical and jurisdictional limits. The decision on the pleaded tort claim also does not automatically answer every question about rescission or a seller’s request for specific performance.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It establishes the baseline that Kannavos qualifies: silence, a half-truth, active concealment, and a special duty to speak are different grounds of analysis.

topics.misrepresentation: The claim involved silence without a separate duty or misleading statement.
topics.assent: The alleged hidden defect raises the limits of relief from an uninformed bargain.
topics.disclosure: The court declined a general duty to reveal latent defects on the pleaded facts.
